title: ICE Plans to Spend Up to $20 Million on Electrical Shock Gloves for Agents
excerpt: The Department of Homeland Security posted a contract notice for G.L.O.V.E. devices that deliver up to 380 volts on skin contact, drawing swift condemnation from civil rights groups.
body:
• ICE plans to spend between $10 million and $20 million on electrical shock gloves called G.L.O.V.E. (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter) for agents and officers.
  • The devices, made by Lexington, Kentucky-based Compliant Technologies LLC, deliver up to 380 volts on skin contact and are marketed as "de-escalation" tools.
  • Civil rights groups including the ACLU have condemned the plan, calling ICE "a rogue agency" equipping officers with "another tool capable of inflicting pain."
  • The contract notice, published on DHS's procurement portal on August 10, calls for delivery by March 31, 2027, with solicitation possible as early as this Friday.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement is planning to equip its agents and officers with gloves that deliver electrical shocks during encounters with individuals, according to a Department of Homeland Security contract notice published this week.

The agency plans to spend between $10 million and $20 million on devices known as CTG 5 G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, according to the notice posted Monday on DHS's Acquisition Planning Forecast System. The devices would be issued to both Homeland Security Investigations and Enforcement and Removal Operations personnel, with delivery expected by March 31, 2027.

What Are the G.L.O.V.E. Devices?

Manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC, a small business incorporated in 2018 in Lexington, Kentucky, the G.L.O.V.E. functions as a regular patrol glove until the wearer presses a switch that activates an electrical current. The device must make direct contact with a person's skin to be effective and does not work through clothing or hair, according to the company's user manual.

The gloves can deliver a maximum voltage of up to 380 volts that "inhibits/distracts the subject from performing coordinated muscle movement," the manual states. The company markets the device as a "wearable de-escalation device" and an "invisible partner" designed to "enhance the user's effectiveness."

"It's immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting."

— John Peters, President, Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths

Peters, who has studied how the device has been used, told the Associated Press that officers typically gain compliance within three seconds. The user manual stipulates that no more than two gloves should be applied to a subject simultaneously and limits use to 15 seconds in most instances.

Prior Use and Concerns

The devices have been used before in law enforcement and corrections settings. In 2024, Oklahoma County Jail began deploying G.L.O.V.E. gloves produced by the same company. The jail's then-CEO said the device was particularly useful for its majority female staff.

But the technology has also been involved in incidents resulting in criminal charges. In 2022, two corrections officers at the Laurens County Detention Center in South Carolina were charged with beating and shocking an inmate with "a wearable G.L.O.V.E. stun device" in separate incidents, according to the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division.

Compliant Technologies has also been sued in federal court. In 2022, a Kentucky man alleged a sheriff's deputy grabbed his arm and shocked him with the gloves while he was shackled and awaiting surgery for a torn bicep tendon.

Civil Rights Groups Sound Alarm

The planned procurement has drawn swift condemnation from civil rights organizations, coming amid ongoing scrutiny of ICE's tactics under the Trump administration's push to carry out roughly 2,000 arrests per day.

"This is a rogue agency with an $80 billion slush fund that allows them to concoct and fund new ways to visit cruelty upon our communities."

— Kica Matos, President, National Immigration Law Center

Eric King, a spokesperson for the ACLU of Kentucky, said in a statement that the organization is "deeply concerned by plans to provide ICE agents with another tool capable of inflicting pain on people in their custody or during enforcement encounters." He questioned whether "an agency exercising extraordinary power over people's freedom and safety should be given increasingly coercive tools without corresponding transparency, oversight and accountability."

Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the national ACLU, warned that "ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do."

What This Means for Immigrants

For the Indian diaspora community, the procurement adds to an already tense environment around immigration enforcement. ICE's expanded use-of-force tools comes as the agency continues aggressive enforcement operations in communities across the country, including in areas with significant South Asian populations.

Compliant Technologies's own guidelines warn against using the gloves on pregnant women, elderly individuals, small children, and severely disabled persons, as well as for "verbal defiance or belligerence." Critics question whether these restrictions will be meaningfully enforced during high-pressure field encounters.

What's Next

The DHS notice indicated that a solicitation for a no-bid contract could be published as early as Friday. Neither DHS nor Compliant Technologies provided substantive comment. A DHS spokesperson said ICE is "constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country."

The Associated Press first reported the contract notice. Jeff Niklaus, founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, said in an email that the company was unable to comment.
